Before commenting on the significance of the Filioque, I just want to comment on your use of the word "aspects" to describe the Three Persons of the Trinity. That sounds to me like the Modalist heresy. In brief, two heretical conceptions of the Trinity can be conceived as the intemperate extremes, between which the true conception of the Trinity lies (the Aristotelian Golden Mean, if you will, or Christ crucified between two thieves). One extreme is conceiving of the Trinity as referring to literally three gods. This is obviously a false conception and little exposition is required to explain why, I think. The less obvious extreme is that of Modalism, which merely asserts that the Trinity represents three modes of One God, rather than there being three distinct hypostases, or Persons, in the Triune God. Modalism might require a complex rather than simple God, I'm not sure on that point - but what matters is that Modalism attempts to reduce the Trinity to something merely descriptive. It is not. The Trinity describes One God in Three Persons - three hypostases with the same Divine Essence. Some Aquinas asks whether it is better to use the word hypostasis or Person, and concludes that Person is much preferred, since hypostasis is flawed / misleading in some sense, though permissible by virtue of the fact that it is the best words the Greeks had to use to describe this very difficult mystery.

Now on to the Filioque. I know it's a lot of reading, but please revisit my quoting of Thomas on this issue (here, here, and here). I think this exposition is actually readily graspable, if read carefully, unlike much of Aquinas which readily escapes understanding even when read multiple times.

He points out how, based on Scripture, the Son of God must have authority over the Holy Spirit, since "all things that are the Father's" are also the Son's, and the Father has authority over the Holy Spirit - the Father can send the Holy Spirit. So too must the Son. As Thomas writes:

[14] Moreover, the Father and the Son, unity of essence considered, do not differ save in this: He is the Father and He is the Son. So, anything other than this is common to the Father and the Son. But to be the principle of the Holy Spirit is not included in the notion of paternity and of sonship, for it is one relation by which the Father is Father, and another by which He is the principle of the Holy Spirit, as was said above. Therefore, to be the principle of the Holy Spirit is common to the Father and the Son.

He points out that, because the Divine Persons are distinguished by relation to each other only, it must be the case that the relations the Son has with the Father and Holy Spirit are different from the relations the Holy Spirit has with the Father and the Son - because if this is not the case, there would be no distinction whatever between Son and Holy Spirit, and thus there would be only Two Persons. Now, if the Son does not send the Holy Spirit also - if the Son is not with the Father in being the principle of origin of the holy Spirit - then both the Son and the Holy Spirit are related identically to the other Two Persons, i.e. the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and not from the Son; the Son proceeds from the Father and not from the Holy Spirit. If B proceeds from A but not C, and C proceeds from A but not B, and relation is the only means of distinguishing A, B, and C, then B and C are equal, which means B = C, which means there is only A and B, which is heresy. So by virtue of the need for distinction between Son and Holy Spirit, the Filioque is essential. Thomas puts it much better than I ever could:

[9] What is more, when things come together by something common to them, they must, if they are to be distinguished, be distinguished by differences which belong per se and not accidentally to that common thing. Thus, man and horse meet in animal, and are distinguished from one another not by black and white, which are related accidentally to animal, but by rational and irrational, which are per se pertinent to animal. This is because animal is what has soul [ animam ], and this must be distinguished by having this or that kind of soul—say, rational or irrational. Now, manifestly, the Son and the Holy Spirit agree in their being from another, since each is from the Father. And in this the Father suitably differs from each, in that He can have no birth-origin [ innascibilis ]. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit be distinguished from the Son, this must take place by differences which per se divide this being from another. And such, indeed, can only be differences of the same genus—namely, pertaining to origin—so that one of them is from the other. One concludes, then, that the distinction of the Holy Spirit from the Son requires that He be from the Son.

The only real reason the Orthodox have for insisting that the Filioque is false, is that it was not explicitly stated in the original Creed. Thus they claim the Latins "added it" later on. To this Thomas has this to say:

[3] They further object that in certain councils one finds it prohibited under penalty of anathema to add anything to the Creed ordered by the council. In this, they say, there is no mention of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. And so they hold the Latins guilty of anathema because they have added this to the Creed.

[4] But such arguments are inefficacious. For the declaration of the Synod of Chalcedon says that the Fathers gathered at Constantinople corroborated the doctrine of the Synod of Nicea. This they did, “not as though to imply that the doctrine was something less, but to declare by Scriptural testimonies the understanding of the Holy Spirit Of their predecessors against those who attempted to reject that understanding.” One must say, similarly, that the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is implicitly contained in the Creed of Constantinople, for the latter says that “He proceeds from the Father,” and what is understood of the Father must be understood of the Son, as was said. And the authority of the Roman Pontiff sufficed for this addition; by this authority, too, all the ancient councils were confirmed.

[5] They maintain, also, that the Holy Spirit, since He is simple, cannot be from two; and that the Holy Spirit, if He proceeds perfectly from the Father, does not proceed from the Son; and other arguments of this sort. These are easy to solve, even if one is but little skilled in theological matters. For the Father and the Son are a single principle of the Holy Spirit by reason of the unity of divine power, and by one production they produce the Holy Spirit; thus, also, the three Persons are one principle of creatures and by one action they produce creatures.

So, Chiro, it is not merely a matter of a vector, like a kite flying in the wind, depending on some visible sign to really know the truth of the matter. This issue of procession is central to an understanding of the Trinity itself - without procession, without distinctions of origin between the Persons, there is no Trinity. Without the Trinity, there is no Christianity. The Trinitarian nature of Christian gnosis is not just what distinguishes it from other sapiential traditions - it is that which renders it fully comprehensible and coherent.

If that does not suffice to indicate the reason that this controversy is actually important, let me reference Thomas again in saying that if a single article of faith is corrupted, the entire faith is corrupted. Rather than going into a lengthy explanation of why this is the case (which I do not at this time fully grasp myself) I will merely compare it to a similar issue. I have written before about how a single evil element in an act corrupts the entire act, even if the act had a good object. So giving alms to the poor can be an evil act if the circumstances are not right (such as, the giver's children are starving), or if the end is evil (the giver gave in order to be perceived as generous, rather than for the glory of God and true charity). Even though giving alms itself, as an object, is good, the fullness of the act can be corrupted if even one of the four elements (subject, object, circumstances, end) is evil. Likewise with faith. If one believes in 99% of the articles of faith, but believes the contrary of 1% of the articles (that is to say, actively holds an heretical view on 1% of the articles of faith), then that person's entire faith is corrupted. Again, this doesn't mean they aren't right about 99% of what they believe; it means that, by virtue of actively believing in something contrary to an article of faith, the entire faith is corrupted. One might believe in the Trinity, understand the proper processions, and get practically everything right in the faith - but if one believes Jesus Christ was just a man, and not Divine, like a mere prophet sent by God; or if one believes Jesus Christ was born a mere man but became God - then how can one say this person holds the true faith? How can this singular false belief not corrupt the coherence and truth of the whole? Even if every other article is believed, a false conception of this singular article renders everything else incomprehensible, in fact, renders it vain ("And if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." - 1 Cor 15:14). It is important to get these things right; Christ gave us a Church so that these articles could be made clear to us by an authority we could trust. It was never meant to be up to individuals to try and figure this out themselves; this is the tragedy of the Protestants (that, and their disbelief in and lack of reception of the Eucharist).

I hope that clarifies things rather than obfuscating them further.
